policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
SUBJECT MATTER
1.1. Reification of Technical Note No. 627/2021-CGPNI/DEIDT/SVS/MS, which deals with guidelines regarding the temporary suspension of vaccination against covid-19 with the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine in pregnant and postpartum women; interruption of vaccination against covid-19 in pregnant and postpartum women without comorbidities and continuation of vaccination against covid-19 in pregnant and postpartum women with comorbidities.
2. ANALYSIS
2.1. In the sixth edition of the National Plan for the Operationalization of Vaccination against Covid-19, pregnant and postpartum women were included as priorities for vaccination against the disease. This inclusion occurred after extensive discussion in the Technical Advisory Chamber on Immunizations and Communicable Diseases and the Technical Advisory Chamber on integrated actions to Assistance to Pregnant Women and Postpartum Women in the context of the new coronavirus pandemic (covid-19), and considered that pregnant and postpartum women (until 45 days after delivery) are at increased risk for developing severe forms of covid-19 as well as resulting obstetric complications, such as premature birth and fetal death (Rasmussen and
Jamieson, 2021).
2.2. This recommendation was also based on the national epidemiological scenario, with high circulation of SARS-CoV-2 and the increase in the number of maternal deaths by covid-19 in 2021. Between January 1 and May 10, 2021, 6,416 cases of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) in pregnant women (257.87 cases per 100,000 pregnant women), of which 4,103 were confirmed as
covid-19 (167.91 cases per 100,000 pregnant women), 38 had another eological diagnosis, 1,248 had no defined diagnosis, and 1,027 were under investigation. Of the total number of SARS cases in pregnant women, 505 died (20.30 deaths per 100,000 pregnant women), 475 of which were confirmed for covid-19
(19.09 deaths per 100,000 pregnant women) (Source: SIVEP-Gripe, May 10, 2021. Data subject to change.).
2.3. After the start of vaccination of the group of pregnant and postpartum women, the National Immunization Program (PNI) received notification of a case of serious adverse event in a pregnant woman after the administration of the COVID-19 AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine. This is an event that occurred in a pregnant woman in the state of Rio de Janeiro, suspected for the Thrombosis Syndrome with Thrombocytopenia (TTS), which has a possible causal association with non-replicating viral vector vaccines. The case was evaluated by the Technical Advisory Board on Pharmacovigilance of Vaccines and Other Immunobiologicals (CTAFAVI), and was classified as level 2 of diagnostic certainty (probable case) according to the criteria of the Brighton collaboration for TTS. Regarding TTS, it is an extremely rare syndrome, initially described in Europe, with an estimated incidence of one case per 100,000 administered doses of the vaccine, and it has not yet been possible to establish risk factors for its occurrence, and the almost all events were reported after the first dose. So far, no cases of this syndrome have been reported in pregnant women worldwide.
2.4. In view of the occurrence of this case, the National Health Surveillance Agency issued a note requesting the interruption of the vaccination of pregnant women using the aforementioned vaccine. The safety and efficacy of the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine has not been fully evaluated in pregnant women. However, animal studies have shown no deleterious effect on pregnancy, and data from inadvertently vaccinated pregnant women have not shown increased risk of complications (Male, 2021). It is noteworthy that the platform used (non-replicating viral vector) does not use viable viruses and, therefore, is not capable of causing the disease in vaccinated individuals. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine be used in pregnant women in scenarios where the benefits outweigh risks. Until 05/10/2021, more than 15 thousand pregnant women had been vaccinated with the vaccine AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz in Brazil (SIPNI), and this was the first serious adverse event reported in this group with a possible causal association with the vaccine.
2.5. Pregnancy itself is a condition with increased risk of thrombosis and bleeding events. However, there is no evidence that it would be a risk factor for the occurrence of TTS. Considering the proposed and specific pathophysiological mechanism for this syndrome (presence of auto-antibodies against platelet factor 4) (Scully et al., 2021), it is not expected that there is an increased risk of occurrence of the syndrome in individuals who have other predisposing factors for thrombosis, including pregnant women. The exception is individuals who had a previous picture of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia.
2.6. With the data available to date, it is highly likely that the benefit risk profile of the vaccine in pregnant women remains favourable. It is noteworthy that the risk of death from covid-19 in pregnant women in Brazil in 2021 was 20 times higher than the risk of occurrence of TTS described in the medical literature. However, given the present fact, considering the need for more safety data on the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine in pregnant women, as a precaution, the PNI chooses, at this time, to temporarily suspend the use of the COVID-19 AstraZeneca/Oxford/ vaccine Fiocruz in pregnant and postpartum women, supported by the recommendations of the Technical Advisory Board on Immunizations and Communicable Diseases and in compliance with Anvisa's request. Additionally, it is recommended to discontinue the vaccination of pregnant and postpartum women without other factors that imply an increased risk for covid-19.
2.7. Vaccination of pregnant and postpartum women should be subject to medical prescription after individualized benefit risk assessment.
2.8. Pregnant women and postpartum women with comorbidities who have not yet been vaccinated should be vaccinated with COVID-19 vaccines that do not contain a viral vector (Sinovac/Butantan or Pfizer/Wyeth).
2.9. Pregnant women and postpartum women (including those without additional risk factors) who have already received the first dose of the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine must wait for the end of the gestation and postpartum period (up to 45 days after delivery) for the administration of the second dose of the vaccine.
2.10. Pregnant women and postpartum women (including those without additional risk factors) who have already received the first dose of another COVID-19 vaccine that does not contain a viral vector (Sinovac/Butantan or Pfizer) should complete the regimen with the same vaccine at the usual intervals.
2.11. Pregnant women and mothers belonging to other priority groups (health workers or other essential services workers, for example) may be vaccinated after an individual risk and benefit assessment to be carried out in conjunction with their doctor.
2.12. Pregnant women and mothers who have already been immunized with the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine should be advised to seek immediate medical care if they present one of the following signs/symptoms within 4 to 28 days following vaccination:
Shortness of breathe.
Chest pain.
Swelling in the leg.
Persistent abdominal pain.
Neurological symptoms such as persistent and severe headache, blurred, difficulty speaking or drowsiness.
Small red spots on the skin beyond where the vaccine was applied.
2.13. Health workers involved in prenatal care should be aware of the immunization history of pregnant women under their care to provide appropriate guidance. In addition, it is recommended to reinforce with pregnant women the need to maintain protective measures even after vaccination.
2.14. Health workers should pay attention to the signs and symptoms of TTS syndrome and recommendations for appropriate management, as detailed in Technical Note No. 441 /2021 -
CGPNI/DEIDT/SVS/MS, available at the link: hps://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/coronavirus/vacinas/planonacional-de-operacionalizacao-da-vacina-contra-a-covid-19
2.15. Suspected cases of the syndrome should be reported in the e-SUS nofica (hps://nofica.saude.gov.br) as adverse events.
2.16. It is noteworthy that these recommendations may be re-evaluated in light of new evidence that may become available.
3. CONCLUSION
3.1. In view of the occurrence of a serious adverse event after vaccination in a pregnant woman vaccinated with the AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine with a possible causal association with the vaccine and in response to a request from Anvisa, the National Immunization Program advises the interruption of the use of COVID-19 AstraZeneca/Oxford/Fiocruz vaccine in pregnant and postpartum women. Additionally, it is recommended to interrupt vaccination of pregnant and postpartum women without other risk factors for covid-19 (for the details of risk factors, see the National Plan for Operationalization of Vaccination Against Covid-19). It is noteworthy, however, that the benefit/risk profile of this vaccine is still highly favorable, and should continue to be used by other groups. Vaccination of pregnant and postpartum women with comorbidities should continue with the use of other COVID-19 vaccines that do not contain a viral vector (Sinovac/Butantan or Pfizer/Wyeth) available in the country.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
10. CAN I GET VACCINATED AGAINST SARS-COV-2 IF I AM PREGNANT / BREASTFEEDING?
For now, data on the use of currently available vaccines against COVID-19 (Comirnaty-Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, Vaxzevria - AstraZeneca, Janssen) in pregnant and lactating women are limited. The data collected so far from preclinical studies do not show a detrimental effect on pregnancy, embryonic and fetal development, childbirth or postnatal development (postpartum development). To date, data from the adverse reaction monitoring system do not indicate a signal of uncertainty in the use of COVID-19 vaccine in pregnant and lactating women. Additionally, data from one large systematic review suggest that pregnant women are more likely to have a more severe clinical picture of COVID-19 disease and to be admitted to intensive care units than women of the same age who are not pregnant. Vaccination of pregnant women should be considered in particular if the pregnant woman is at higher risk of exposure to SARS-CoV-2 infection (healthcare professional, higher incidence rate in the environment…) or higher risk of consequences of COVID-19 (chronic disease, old age). Therefore, if a pregnant woman wants to protect herself against COVID-19, she should be allowed to do so because, despite limited information so far, vaccination is not contraindicated.

Also, although data on the effects of vaccination on breastfeeding are limited for the time being, breastfeeding is not a contraindication to vaccination.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Can you get a COVID-19 vaccine while pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding?
Vaccines are generally considered safe during pregnancy if they do not contain live viruses. The new mRNA and adenovirus vector COVID-19 vaccines do not contain live viruses, but, as of yet, they have not been systematically researched on people who are pregnant.  

The attending physician may, at their discretion, recommend a mRNA vaccination during pregnancy provided that the person is willing to be vaccinated and belongs to a risk group for COVID-19 due to an underlying condition or has a significant risk of being exposed to the virus at work, for example. 

COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy does not cause any particular concern or require more detailed foetal diagnostic studies. Despite the limited number of studies on pregnant women, it is presumed that the vaccination would not harm the pregnancy or the foetus. In several countries where the COVID-19 vaccination programme began earlier than in Finland, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, pregnant women have also been vaccinated on the basis of individual discretion. Data will gradually accumulate from these countries that we can also utilise in Finland.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
Can you get a COVID-19 vaccine while pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding?
You can get a COVID-19 vaccination during breastfeeding. The messenger RNA contained in the vaccine is destroyed in the body within 24 hours, and it is unlikely that it would pass into breast milk. Also the ingredients of the adenovirus vector have a short life span and are not known to transfer to human breast milk.

In addition, the country intends to extend vaccination to the prison population and to persons aged 16 to 49 constituting the national phase. The population of this phase is estimated at 13,976,093 or about 49.3% of the total population. Operational costs and vaccines relating to this phase will be supported by the country and its partners.
In sum, the total target population for vaccination against COVID-19 estimated at 19,645,908 or about 69.3% of the total population.
NB: Pregnant and breastfeeding women are not affected by this vaccination by precautionary principle.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
If you are pregnant, 18 years of age or older, you have the right to receive the COVID-19 vaccine from the ninth week of pregnancy.

Today we know that during pregnancy you can have serious complications from COVID-19 that warrant hospitalization, admission to intensive care units and the need for mechanical ventilation, conditions that increase the risk of dying from COVID-19.

Severe cases of COVID-19 in pregnant women usually appear from the second trimester and as the age of the pregnant person increases, compared to non-pregnant or those in the first trimester.

Follow the hygiene measures, healthy distance, use the mouth cover and receive the vaccine against COVID-19, protect your health.

You can get the COVID-19 vaccine regardless of your social security type.

Frequent questions
If I am pregnant, should I get the COVID-19 vaccine?
In Mexico, vaccination is voluntary and free. The COVID-19 vaccine provides greater protection at this stage, and is recommended from 18 years of age and from the ninth week of pregnancy.

What are the risks for pregnant women if they get COVID-19?
Today we know that pregnant women are at higher risk for developing severe forms of COVID-19 that require hospitalization. This risk increases with age, especially after 30 years, from the second trimester, or in pregnant women with overweight, diabetes, hypertension or heart and respiratory diseases.

What are the benefits of getting vaccinated against COVID?
In studies conducted, vaccines are shown to be 65-90% effective in preventing symptomatic or severe cases of COVID-19. Therefore, like any vaccine, they have a high level of protection.

Is the vaccine safe in pregnancy?
No major adverse effects have been shown in pregnant women who have been vaccinated in other countries and the benefits have been shown to outweigh any possible risks. The Mexican Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics Colleges, international expert groups and the Ministry of Health recommend vaccination against COVID-19 in pregnant women. 

Which of the vaccines will I receive if I am pregnant?
All available vaccines can be given to pregnant women. You are in Mexico include:  AstraZeneca,  Cansino, Pfizer-BionTech, Sinovac and  Sputnik V . 


What side effects can I get from the vaccine?
The most commonly reported side effects are injection site pain, tiredness, headache; less often chills or fever and muscle pain. These can happen in pregnant women, as in any population group. If you have persistent or severe symptoms up to 30 days after the vaccination, call 800.0044.800

If the mother is vaccinated against COVID-19, is the fetus vaccinated?
Vaccines activate the body's natural defenses to resist specific infections, and strengthen the immune system; Some studies indicate that when vaccinated against COVID-19 during pregnancy, the mother's immunity would protect the product of pregnancy until the first weeks of birth, although research on this continues.


If I get vaccinated during pregnancy, will I be able to breastfeed my baby?
The vaccine does not prevent you from starting breastfeeding. Breastfeeding is recommended from birth, exclusively for the first six months of life and complementary until two years of age.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Can you get a COVID-19 vaccine while pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding?
Vaccines are generally considered safe during pregnancy if they do not contain live viruses. The new mRNA and adenovirus vector COVID-19 vaccines do not contain live viruses, but, as of yet, they have not been systematically researched on people who are pregnant.  

The attending physician may, at their discretion, recommend a mRNA vaccination during pregnancy provided that the person is willing to be vaccinated and belongs to a risk group for COVID-19 due to an underlying condition or has a significant risk of being exposed to the virus at work, for example. 

COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy does not cause any particular concern or require more detailed foetal diagnostic studies. Despite the limited number of studies on pregnant women, it is presumed that the vaccination would not harm the pregnancy or the foetus. In several countries where the COVID-19 vaccination programme began earlier than in Finland, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, pregnant women have also been vaccinated on the basis of individual discretion. Data will gradually accumulate from these countries that we can also utilise in Finland.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
Can you get a COVID-19 vaccine while pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding?
You can get a COVID-19 vaccination during breastfeeding. The messenger RNA contained in the vaccine is destroyed in the body within 24 hours, and it is unlikely that it would pass into breast milk. Also the ingredients of the adenovirus vector have a short life span and are not known to transfer to human breast milk.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
What about vaccinating pregnant women?
There are currently few data on the vaccination of pregnant women with covid-19 vaccines, which do not indicate that vaccination would be harmful to pregnant women, the fetus or the newborn. In pregnant women, covid-19 disease may be more severe. Vaccination of pregnant women can be done after careful consideration of the benefits and risks. This is particularly important in pregnant women at risk for severe covida-19 and in pregnant women who are more exposed to the infection (eg healthcare professionals). There are no reservations about vaccination after childbirth. Given the available data on the safety and efficacy of mRNA vaccines in pregnant women and the absence of these data for other vaccines, it is recommended that pregnant women be vaccinated with mRNA vaccines.
If a woman who has received the first dose of Vaxzevria (AstraZeneca) becomes pregnant, the mRNA vaccine (4 to 12 weeks after receiving the dose of Vaxzevria) can be used for the 2nd dose. One dose of covid-19 vaccine is sufficient to protect pregnant women who have been shown to have covid-19 in the last 8 months.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
What about vaccinating breastfeeding mothers?
Vaccination against covid-19 is equally recommended for breastfeeding mothers as well as for non-breastfeeding individuals.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Pregnant women can get vaccinated with the mRNA vaccines from Pfizer and Moderna. This no longer applies only to women with underlying diseases (such as diabetes or heart and lung diseases), but also to healthy pregnant women. The benefits of vaccination outweigh the possible disadvantages. 

Vaccination during pregnancy
Pregnant women are more likely to become seriously ill from the corona virus than non-pregnant women. Pregnant women with an underlying disease (such as diabetes or heart and lung diseases) are especially at higher risk. Therefore, the advice until now has been to only vaccinate pregnant women with underlying diseases. We now know that 90,000 pregnant women in the United States have been vaccinated with the mRNA vaccines from Pfizer-BioNtech and Moderna. No serious side effects have been reported. From now on, therefore, all pregnant women are advised to undergo a vaccination if they are called upon to do so, preferably with an mRNA vaccine.

More information about vaccination against COVID-19 around pregnancy can be found on the website of the Dutch Association for Obstetrics and Gynecology ( NVOG Dutch Association for Obstetrics and Gynecology ).

mRNA vaccines and pregnancy
The Pfizer-BioNtech and Moderna vaccines against COVID-19 are mRNA vaccines. Based on the mechanism of action and the data obtained in the meantime on these vaccines, there is no reason to believe that these vaccines against COVID-19 would be harmful when used during pregnancy.

Not enough is currently known about the safety of Janssen's vaccine during pregnancy. AstraZeneca's vaccine is used for people over 60 years of age.

If you are vaccinated during your pregnancy, we request that you participate in Mothers of Tomorrow. Mothers of Tomorrow (part of the Lareb side effects center National Registration Evaluation Side Effects  ) is researching the safety of vaccinations and medicines during pregnancy. You can register via www.moedersvanmorgen.nl.

Protection of baby after mother vaccination
Newborn babies are protected against infectious diseases by the antibodies they receive from their mothers through the placenta. These antibodies slowly disappear in the months after birth. We do not yet know whether this is also the case for the antibodies after corona vaccination, but that seems plausible. 


No effect on the pill or other contraceptives 
Vaccines do not affect the effectiveness of the pill or other contraceptives. And conversely, the pill or other contraceptives do not affect the effectiveness of the vaccine.

There is no evidence that the vaccine passes into breast milk and can reach the child through breast milk.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Pregnant women
Pregnant women are at higher risk of severe COVID-19 compared with women of childbearing age who are not pregnant, and COVID-19 has been associated with an increased risk of preterm birth. The available data on AZD1222 vaccination of pregnant women are insufficient to assess vaccine efficacy or vaccine-associated risks in pregnancy. However, it should be noted that AZD1222 is a nonreplicating vaccine.
Animal developmental and reproductive toxicity (DART) studies are ongoing. Preliminary findings show no indication of harm to the development of the foetus. Further studies are planned in pregnant women in the coming months, including a pregnancy sub-study and a pregnancy registry. As data from these studies become available, recommendations on vaccination will be updated accordingly. In the interim, pregnant women should receive AZD 1222 only if the benefit of vaccination to the pregnant woman outweighs the potential vaccine risks, such as if they are health workers at high risk of exposure or have comorbidities that place them in a high-risk group for severe COVID-19. Information and, if possible, counselling on the lack of safety data for pregnant women should be provided.
WHO does not recommend pregnancy testing prior to vaccination
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
Lactating women
Breastfeeding offers substantial health benefits to lactating women and their breastfed children. Vaccine efficacy is expected to be similar in lactating women as in other adults. It is unknown whether AZD1222 is excreted in human milk. As the AZD1222 vaccine is a non-replicating vaccine, it is unlikely to pose a risk to the breastfeeding child. On the basis of these considerations, a lactating woman who is part of a group recommended for vaccination, e.g., health workers, should be offered vaccination on an equivalent basis. WHO does not recommend discontinuing breastfeeding after vaccination

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Individuals who are pregnant or breastfeeding
Evidence regarding the safety and immunogenicity of COVID-19 vaccines in individuals who are pregnant or breastfeeding are emerging. Pre-clinical studies on the safety of COVID-19 vaccines
from animal developmental and reproductive toxicity studies did not identify concerns regarding female reproduction, fetal/embryonal development, or postnatal development following the
administration of the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine prior to or during gestation (79). A report presented to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) also did not indicate adverse effects with respect to fertility, pregnancy, embryo/fetal development, or postnatal development (up to day 21) in studies in rats using a full dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine (80). A US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) review of a study in rabbits that received the Janssen COVID-19
vaccine at two times the human dose prior to or during gestation similarly concluded there were no adverse effects on female reproduction, fetal/embryonal development, or postnatal
development (81). AstraZeneca performed a preliminary DART study in 32 female mice given the vaccine prior to or during gestation and found no effects of female reproduction, fetal or pup survival or development. Their main DART study in mice is ongoing (82).
Analysis of data collected through international COVID-19 immunization registries to date have not revealed any maternal or neonatal safety signals, and preliminary analyses of over 35,000
pregnant women in the United States who received an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine did not reveal any obvious safety signals (83) In one small cohort study, mRNA from COVID-19 vaccines was undetectable in breastmilk 4-48 hours post-vaccination (84).
Emerging evidence suggests that COVID-19 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy is also immunogenic and results in comparable antibody titres to those generated in non-pregnant women (85)(86)(87). Maternal IgG humoral response to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines transfers across the placenta to the fetus, leading to a significant and potentially protective, antibody titre in the neonatal bloodstream one week after the second dose (88)(85)(89, 90). Observational studies consistently show that both anti-spike IgG and IgA are present in breastmilk for at least 6 weeks after maternal vaccination with mRNA vaccines.

Pregnancy and Breastfeeding
10. NACI preferentially recommends that a complete vaccine series with an mRNA COVID19 vaccine should be offered to individuals in the authorized age group who are pregnant. If an mRNA vaccine is contraindicated, another authorized COVID-19 vaccine should be offered. Informed consent should include discussion about emerging
evidence on the safety of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in this population. (Strong NACI Recommendation)
11. NACI recommends that a complete series with a viral vector COVID-19 vaccine may be offered to individuals 30 years of age and older who are pregnant if the conditions outlined in Recommendation #2 (above) are met AND a risk assessment deems the benefits outweigh the potential risks for the individual and the fetus (considering concerns about possible complexities of treatment of VITT in pregnancy, should it occur). Informed consent should include discussion about limited evidence on the use of viral vector vaccines in this population. (Discretionary NACI Recommendation)
12. NACI recommends that a complete vaccine series with an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine should be offered to individuals in the authorized age group who are breastfeeding. If an mRNA vaccine is contraindicated, another authorized COVID-19 vaccine should be offered. Informed consent should include discussion about the emerging evidence on the safety of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in this population. (Strong NACI Recommendation)
13. NACI recommends that a complete series with a viral vector COVID-19 vaccine may be offered to individuals 30 years of age and older who are breastfeeding if the conditions outlined in Recommendation #2 (above) are met. Informed consent should include discussion about the limited evidence on the use of viral vector vaccines in this population. (Discretionary NACI Recommendation)
 
Summary of evidence and rationale
 Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals were excluded from the mRNA and viral vector COVID-19 clinical trials. However, outcomes in participants who became pregnant during the clinical trials and fetal outcomes are reported through registries, and real-world evidence (mostly with mRNA vaccination) has become available.
 An mRNA vaccine is preferred due to published safety data. Recently published preliminary analyses of 35,691 pregnant women in the United States who received an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine did not reveal any obvious safety signals (83). If VITT were to occur after receipt of a viral vector vaccine in a pregnant person, there might be complexity
in the medical care. The US safety data suggests mRNA vaccine administration within 30 days of conception is safe (83). Those who are trying to become pregnant do not need to avoid pregnancy after vaccination with an mRNA vaccine.
 Analysis of data collected through international COVID-19 immunization registries to date have not revealed any maternal or neonatal safety signals.
 To date, no safety signals have been detected in Development and Reproductive Toxicity (DART) animal studies for Pfizer(80), Moderna(79), Janssen(99), and AstraZeneca vaccines (82).
 Emerging evidence suggests that COVID-19 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy results in comparable antibody titres to those generated in non-pregnant women (85) (86) (87).
Maternal IgG humoral response to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines transfers across the placenta to the fetus, leading to a significant and potentially protective, antibody titre in the neonatal bloodstream one week after the second dose (88) (85) (89) (90).
 Observational studies consistently show that both anti-spike IgG and IgA are present in breastmilk at least for 6 weeks after maternal vaccination with mRNA vaccines (91)(92)(93)(94)(100)(101)(84)(102).
 In one small cohort study, mRNA from COVID-19 vaccines was undetectable in breastmilk 4-48 hours post-vaccination. No safety signals have been detected with mRNA vaccination during breastfeeding and individuals should continue to breastfeed after
vaccination (84).
 The evidence of pregnancy as an independent risk factor for severe COVID-19 is evolving. A rapid review of evidence from OECD member countries found a low certainty of evidence of at least a two-fold increase in hospitalization due to COVID-19 for pregnancy (any stage) and a low certainty of evidence for little to no increase in mortality. Caution should be taken when interpreting low certainty evidence. However, the review found a moderate certainty of evidence of at least a two-fold increase in hospitalization and mortality if an individual had two or more underlying medical conditions, compared to individuals with no comorbidities. No direct evidence on the combination of medical conditions associated with increased risk was found (4, 5).
 Compared to non-pregnant persons, SARS-CoV-2 infection in pregnancy may increase the risk of complications requiring hospitalization and intensive care, premature birth and ceasarean delivery. A review of 438,548 pregnant individuals found pregnancy is a risk factor for poorer pregnancy outcomes, such as preeclampsia, pre-term birth, and stillbirth, and that these risks are much greater with severe infection (103). Canadian-based surveillance of COVID-19 in pregnancy in five provinces from March 1st-December 21st, 2020 with a sample of 1880 pregnant positive cases, saw an increased risk of being hospitalized (RR=5.33, 95% CI: 4.51-6.20) and an increased risk of being admitted to the ICU (RR=5.88, 95% CI: 3.80 to 8.22) compared to non-pregnant counterparts (104).
Ventilatory support in pregnancy is more challenging and the risks are greater to both mother and child.
 Vaccine recipients and health care providers are encouraged to enroll patients who have received a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy in COVID-19 vaccine pregnancy registries (refer to Appendix F for a list of COVID-19 vaccine pregnancy registries). Timely reporting on adverse events following immunization to the local public health authority, as
well as to the vaccine manufacturer, for follow up in these vaccine recipients is strongly encouraged.
 NACI encourages research on COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy and during breastfeeding. 
NACI will monitor the evidence as it evolves, and update recommendations as needed

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Is vaccination allowed / recommended for pregnant women? If so, how will vaccination affect the fetus?

Pregnant women were not included in the early COVID-19 vaccine studies, but some participants were either pregnant and did not know about it at the time or became pregnant during the study. Consequently, there are incomplete data on vaccination of pregnant women. The good news is that no side effects were found in this small group of women and the vaccine worked. But more data is needed on the use of the vaccine in a larger number of pregnant women. Several specific medical institutions have come up with recommendations that pregnant women, who are part of a recommended group, receive the COVID-19 vaccine if they choose to do so. First, some pregnant women are at increased risk of COVID-19 infection, such as health care workers or those with certain health conditions. Second, pregnant women are at increased risk of developing complications compared to non-pregnant women when infected with COVID-19. All pregnant women should take these two important points into account: Pregnant women who decide to receive the COVID-19 vaccine should be monitored by their doctor. Also, whether a pregnant woman decides to get vaccinated or not, she must strictly follow the recommended public health measures.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
Is vaccination allowed for nursing mothers?
Although breastfeeding women have not been included in clinical trials, current data suggest that COVID-19 is not transmitted through breast milk. On the other hand, some breastfeeding women will have a higher risk of exposure so they may benefit from the vaccine. It is recommended that women do not delay breast-feeding for any time after being vaccinated. The baby may also benefit from antibodies or immune cells that can be introduced through breast milk after the mother has been vaccinated. This is called passive immunity.

policies.preConceptionRecommendationFreeText:
Given the existence of limited data on this subject and that the existing animal data do not show the impact of vaccination in the pre-conceptual phase, the CSS does not object to the systematic vaccination of women of old age. childbearing and wishing to become pregnant, all the more so for healthcare workers at high risk of exposure and women with co-morbidities placing them in a high-risk group for severe COVID-19 (see opinion CSS-9618 ).
In addition, the CSS is following in the footsteps of the BSRM and the FAMHP by recommending a complete vaccination against COVID-19 before PMA12, thus emphasizing that PMA is not a contraindication to the administration of vaccines against COVID -19 (BSRM, 2021; FAMHP, 2021). In humans, a recent study on a sufficiently representative sample showed that the vaccine had no impact on the spermogram (volume, concentration, motility) (Safrai et al., 2021).

If pregnancy should occur after the first vaccination, the second dose will be given. The administration of one of the vaccines is therefore absolutely not an indication of termination of pregnancy. In fact, it is useful in this regard to recall that this is not a question of live attenuated viral vaccines and that there is no basis for suspecting that they may induce fetal anomalies (Donders F. et al. al, 2020; CSS 8754 “Vaccination of pregnant women”).
It is also advisable to follow the recommendations for reporting post-vaccine side effects as recommended in official procedures.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Contrary to previous recommendations and on the basis of scientific data and the most recent recommendations, the CSS considers that all pregnant women should ideally be vaccinated as a priority (phase Ib of the campaign), and this compared to a woman not pregnant due to increased risk of severe COVID-19 to the mother and premature delivery.
In addition, the CSS reaffirms that the mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 currently available can be administered safely to pregnant women.These vaccines will be administered to all pregnant women regardless of their age (over or under 41 years) and regardless of the trimester of pregnancy (in analogy with the recommendations of Opinion 8754 on influenza vaccination).
The SHC recommended that, for anyone who has already received a first dose of Vaxzevria® vaccine, the interval for the administration of the second vaccine dose be extended by 4 weeks (therefore 16 weeks after the first dose).
The CSS points out that the presence of comorbidity (s) such as increased BMI before pregnancy, hypertension, diabetes, etc. is an additional argument for recommending this vaccination in pregnant women (see opinion CSS-9618).
In cases of increased risk of infection, such as in healthcare workers, vaccination is strongly recommended.
Given the small number of people concerned, the transfer of prioritization of vaccination for pregnant women in phase 1b of the campaign will not significantly impact the vaccination of people aged 45 to 64 without comorbidity. As a reminder, in these people, age (the main driver of the COVID-19 epidemic) also alone represents an increased risk of infection, hospitalization (in ICU11) or death.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
For mothers who are breastfeeding
Although there is no data on the passage into breast milk of vaccine mRNA or Spike proteins, these two elements - if they were to pass into breast milk - would likely be destroyed in the human digestive tract. newborn (mRNA) and / or have no deleterious effect (Spike protein).
In the recent EMA report (point 5.8.1), it is stated there that no particular risk is envisaged during breastfeeding (based on biological plausibilities) with mRNA vaccines (Pfizer / Moderna).
Despite the lack of clinical data available on the subject, the plausibility of a toxic effect in breast-fed children is low, if not nonexistent. As stated in the latest WHO recommendations, the SHC has no particular concerns on this subject.
All lactating women can therefore be vaccinated with all currently available vaccines (4).

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Vaccination during pregnancy and lactation1
As of the date of this document, there are no efficacy and safety studies related to the administration of the vaccine in this population, so there is not enough evidence available to recommend the routine use of the vaccine in pregnant or lactating women before the just being under this condition.
Some important considerations:
 If the vaccine is administered by mistake to a pregnant or lactating woman, it is not recommended to interrupt either of the two situations (neither pregnancy, nor breastfeeding). The programmatic error must be notified for the correct follow-up of the vaccinated person.
 Prevaccination pregnancy tests are not recommended.
...
1,2,3 Special considerations for pregnant women, lactating women, immunocompromised people or people with autoimmune diseases that belong to the prioritized target population for vaccination:
The National Immunization Commission (CoNaIn), in consensus with various Scientific Societies and experts outside the National Ministry of Health, and in line with the analyzes and recommendations published in recent weeks in other countries, have recommended the Ministry of Health to exclude the concept of "contraindication for vaccination against COVID-19" to pregnant women, women who are breastfeeding, immunocompromised people or people with autoimmune diseases that are part of the groups that belong to the target population to be vaccinated (as long as the platform of the vaccine used is NOT live and attenuated viruses).
In this sense, those who are pregnant, lactating women, immunocompromised people or people with autoimmune diseases can choose to be vaccinated, who also:
 present a high risk of exposure to SARS-CoV-2 infection, and that it cannot be avoided: health personnel, strategic personnel, teaching and non-teaching staff (initial, primary and secondary level).
 present 60 years or more and / or people with underlying diseases that include them within “-” or obesity grade 2 or greater (BMI greater than or equal to 35 kg / m2), and / or chronic kidney, respiratory or heart diseases.

This recommendation is based on the need to carry out an individualized evaluation of the benefit that vaccination can offer in these special conditions (pregnancy, lactation, immunocompromise and autoimmune diseases) in the case of high-risk populations, taking into account that:
 the risk of presenting serious adverse events is very unlikely (as they are not live and attenuated virus platforms).
 the contraindication to vaccination in a population at risk due to a lack -fundamentally- of evidence in relation to vaccine efficacy in these special conditions, would expose the individual to a high epidemiological risk, considering their greater vulnerability.
For these cases, interaction or prior consultation with qualified health personnel is also recommended to provide pertinent information prior to the act of vaccination, in order to prioritize the personal and individual decision to receive the vaccine, evaluating the benefit offered by vaccination in in relation to the potential risk of receiving it, and knowing the current conditions in which scientific knowledge is found in relation to safety and efficacy data. Subsequent clinical follow-up is also recommended, if you decide to get vaccinated.

 present 60 years or more and / or people with underlying diseases that include them within “-” or obesity grade 2 or greater (BMI greater than or equal to 35 kg / m2), and / or chronic kidney, respiratory or heart diseases.

This recommendation is based on the need to carry out an individualized evaluation of the benefit that vaccination can offer in these special conditions (pregnancy, lactation, immunocompromise and autoimmune diseases) in the case of high-risk populations, taking into account that:
 the risk of presenting serious adverse events is very unlikely (as they are not live and attenuated virus platforms).
 the contraindication to vaccination in a population at risk due to a lack -fundamentally- of evidence in relation to vaccine efficacy in these special conditions, would expose the individual to a high epidemiological risk, considering their greater vulnerability.
For these cases, interaction or prior consultation with qualified health personnel is also recommended to provide pertinent information prior to the act of vaccination, in order to prioritize the personal and individual decision to receive the vaccine, evaluating the benefit offered by vaccination in in relation to the potential risk of receiving it, and knowing the current conditions in which scientific knowledge is found in relation to safety and efficacy data. policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Background
Pregnant women are at higher risk of severe COVID-19 compared with women of childbearing
age who are not pregnant, and COVID-19 has been associated with an increased risk of
preterm birth. This document offers some preliminary recommendations on the use of the
Janssen Ad26.COV2.S (COVID-19) vaccine in pregnant or lactating women in the context of
the Sisonke trial and in the future national rollout of the Janssen COVID-19 vaccine. These
recommendations consider the safety of the vaccine including the recent reports of Vaccine
induced Thrombotic Thrombocytopaenia (VITT).
Janssen Ad26.COV2.S (COVID-19) vaccine
The Ad26.COV2.S vaccine against COVID-19 is a recombinant, replication-incompetent
adenovirus serotype 26 (Ad26) vector encoding a full-length and stabilized SARS-CoV-2 spike
protein. This vaccine does not contain adjuvants, preservatives, materials of animal origin, or
foetal tissue. A single dose of Ad26.COV2.S has an efficacy of 66.9% (95% confidence interval
(CI): 59.0,73.4) against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection, 76.7% (95% CI: 54.6, 89.1) against
severe COVID-19 disease after 14 days, and 85.4% (95% CI: 54.2, 96.9) after day 28 . Vaccine
efficacy against hospitalisations was 93.1% (95% CI: 72.7, 99.2). Vaccines that use the same
viral vector have been given to pregnant people in all trimesters of pregnancy, including in a
large-scale Ebola vaccination trial. No adverse pregnancy-related outcomes, including adverse
outcomes that affected the infant, were associated with vaccination in these trials.
Clinical data on pregnant and lactating women
While caution about the inclusion of pregnant and lactating women in early clinical trials,
evaluating new vaccines is common, there is a growing global realisation that pregnant and
lactating women should be included in clinical trials at an early and safe point in product
development so that they are not excluded from subsequent use of the product. In addition,
other vaccines are specifically recommended during pregnancy because of the heightened
risk of harm to mother and /or her infant. These include vaccines for influenza, pertussis and
tetanus, with Group B Streptococcal vaccines and Respiratory Syncytial Virus vaccines in
development.
The initial clinical trials of COVID-19 vaccines excluded women who are pregnant, and most
studies excluded women who were lactating. In evaluating the use of COVID-19 vaccines in
pregnant and lactating women consideration must be given to all relevant data including
reproductive developmental toxicity studies, vaccine related adverse effects on female
fertility, embryo-fetal or postnatal development and available clinical data. 
Page | 2
The only direct evidence that can be accessed at this stage would come from inadvertent
administration of COVID-19 vaccines to pregnant women who were inadvertently included in
clinical trials protocols, and particularly from those women who were subsequently enrolled
in pregnancy registries. Other data are emerging from routine rollouts across the globe and
reporting to post-marketing surveillance pregnancy registries. One such set of data was
reported in the NEJM by Shimabukuro et al., 2021 drawing on the CDC v-safe COVID-19
Pregnancy Registry.
Janssen currently states the following in relation to the COVID-19 vaccine
Available data on Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine administered to pregnant women are insufficient
to inform vaccine-associated risks in pregnancy. In a reproductive developmental toxicity
study female rabbits were administered 1 mL of the Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine (a single
human dose is 0.5 mL) by intramuscular injection 7 days prior to mating and on Gestation
Days 6 and 20 (i.e., one vaccination during early and late gestation, respectively). No vaccine
related adverse effects on female fertility, embryo-fetal or postnatal development up to
Postnatal Day 28 were observed.
Data are not available to assess the effects of Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine on the breastfed
infant or on milk production/excretion.
Reports of adverse events following use of the Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine
According to Janssen, reports of adverse events following use of the Janssen COVID-19
vaccine under emergency use authorization in the United States suggest an increased risk of
thrombosis involving the cerebral venous sinuses and other sites (including but not limited to
the large blood vessels of the abdomen and the veins of the lower extremities) combined with
thrombocytopenia and with onset of symptoms approximately one to two weeks after
vaccination. Most cases of thrombosis with thrombocytopenia reported following the Janssen
COVID-19 Vaccine have occurred in females ages 18 through 49 years; some have been fatal.
The clinical course of these events shares features with autoimmune heparin-induced
thrombocytopenia.
SAHPRA’s review of the data generated to date from the Sisonke trial confirm that no cases
of VITT have been identified but there have been some reported cases of thrombosis thought
by the research team not to be associated with the use of the vaccine.
Current WHO recommendations
The available data on Ad26.COV2.S of pregnant women are insufficient to assess vaccineassociated risks in pregnancy. However, it should be noted that Ad26.COV2.S is a
nonreplicating vaccine. No safety issues have been identified following vaccination of more
than 1,600 pregnant women using the Ad26 vaccine platform for vaccines against other
pathogens, such as the Ebola virus. Animal developmental and reproductive toxicity studies
show no harm to the development of the foetus. Further studies are planned in pregnant
women in the coming months, including a pregnancy sub-study and a pregnancy registry. As
data from these studies become available, recommendations on vaccination will be updated
accordingly. In the interim, pregnant women should receive Ad26.COV2.S only if the benefit
of vaccination to the pregnant woman outweighs the potential vaccine risks, such as if the 
Page | 3
woman is a health worker at high risk of exposure or has comorbidities that place them in a
high-risk group for severe COVID-19. Information and, if possible, counselling on the lack of
safety data on Ad26.COV2.S vaccine for pregnant women and the potential benefit of
vaccination should be provided. WHO does not recommend pregnancy testing prior to
vaccination. WHO does not recommend delaying pregnancy because of vaccination.
Breastfeeding offers substantial health benefits to lactating women and their breastfed
children. Vaccine efficacy is expected to be similar in lactating women as in other adults. It is
unknown whether Ad26.COV2.S is excreted in human milk. As the Ad26.COV2.S vaccine is a
non-replicating vaccine, it is unlikely to pose a risk to the breastfeeding child. On the basis of
these considerations, a lactating woman who is part of a group recommended for vaccination,
e.g., health workers, should be offered vaccination on an equivalent basis. WHO does not
recommend discontinuing breastfeeding after vaccination.
Two recent commentaries published in the SAMJ, by Moodley et al. and Zamparini et al. have
accordingly called for a more enabling, individualised and patient-centred approach to the
question. Their conclusions are, respectively:
• “We therefore highly recommend that pregnant women, especially those with
comorbidities, are vaccinated, as COVID-19 poses a risk not only to maternal health
but to fetal viability as well.”
• “While the theoretical benefit of maternal vaccination may outweigh the known risks
associated with COVID-19 in pregnancy, pregnant and breastfeeding women have the
right to autonomy and should be given the choice to vaccinate by making an informed
decision in consultation with their healthcare provider, using the data available.”
in addition, the VMAC recommends the use COVID-19 vaccines in pregnant women, based
on individual benefit -risk assessments, counselling and informed consent.



Conclusions/Recommendations
....
• Pregnant women at high risk of exposure to SARS-CoV-2 (e.g., health workers) or who
have comorbidities which add to their risk of severe COVID-19 disease may be
vaccinated in consultation with their health care provider
• Vaccination data should be collected as part of the ongoing Sisonke Study and by
national pregnancy exposure registries once the vaccine is being rolled out.

Summary of evidence and rationale:

The evidence of pregnancy as an independent risk factor for severe COVID-19 is evolving.
Currently, there are no data on the safety and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines in pregnancy or during breastfeeding. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals were excluded from the mRNA and viral vector COVID-19 vaccine clinical trials.
Currently, there are no data to inform outcomes of inadvertent administration of COVID-19 vaccine to pregnant individuals or their developing fetus in clinical trials. Outcomes in participants who became pregnant during the clinical trials and fetal outcomes will be reported through registries and NACI will reconsider recommendations when these data become available.
It is unknown whether the vaccines are excreted in human milk, but there are no data on outcomes in breastfeeding individuals or their breastfed infants. There have been no theoretical concerns about these vaccines in breastfeeding individuals or their breastfed infants.
Currently, there are limited data on the safety of COVID-19 vaccine from animal developmental and reproductive toxicity studies. In rats that received the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine prior to or during gestation, no safety concerns regarding female reproduction, fetal/embryonal development, or postnatal development were demonstrated. Developmental and Reproductive Toxicity (DART) animal studies for the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine and AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine are ongoing.
Individuals who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or of reproductive age may be at increased risk of exposure to SARS-CoV-2 (e.g., healthcare or essential workers) and/or at increased risk of severe COVID-19 disease (e.g., due to pre-existing medical condition, body mass index of 40 or more) and may wish to be vaccinated despite the lack of evidence of COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy or during breastfeeding in order to protect themselves. Therefore, the balance of benefits and risks must be made on a case-by-case basis.
There is currently no evidence to guide the time interval between the completion of the COVID-19 vaccine series and conception. In the face of scientific uncertainty, it may be prudent to delay pregnancy by 28 days or more after the administration of the complete two-dose vaccine series of a COVID-19 vaccine. A COVID-19 vaccine may be administered any time after pregnancy.
Individuals who become pregnant during their vaccine series or shortly thereafter should not be counselled to terminate pregnancy based on having received a COVID-19 vaccine.
If pregnancy is determined after initiation of the vaccination series, completion of the series may be delayed until after pregnancy, unless risk factors for increased exposure or severe COVID-19 are present and informed consent for vaccination is obtained as above. NACI also encourages additional research and surveillance of COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy.
Eligible individuals should be offered a complete vaccine series with an authorized COVID-19 vaccine post-partum and prior to attempting pregnancy so that the recommended interval between completion of the vaccine series and conception is maintained.
Vaccine recipients and health care providers are encouraged to report to COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy or breastfeeding to the local public health authority as well as to the vaccine manufacturer for follow-up. Active surveillance in these vaccine recipients is strongly encouraged. NACI will monitor the evidence as it evolves and update recommendations as needed.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
VACCINATION OF PREGNANT WOMEN
In consideration of the new knowledge in relation to the vaccination of pregnant women, the updating of national and international recommendations, the specific national epidemiological situation of pregnant women, and bearing in mind the regulatory aspects, the vaccination of pregnant women should consider the following aspects:
1. Population: Pregnant women in the 2nd trimester of pregnancy:
* Pregnant women from 16 weeks of gestational age
2. Prioritization:
* Risk of serious morbidity: in case of presenting comorbidities such as obesity (body mass index> 30), Hypertensive Syndrome of pregnancy, pregestational and gestational diabetes, thrombophilias, multiple pregnancy, pathologies that require immunosuppressive treatment or serious heart or lung diseases.
* Work functions that expose her to increased risk of infection (health personnel, education workers, direct attention to the public, tasks that do not allow Telework).
3. Counseling: Joint evaluation, between the health professional (midwife, nurse or doctor) and the pregnant woman, of the risk / benefit of vaccination against COVID-19. If the benefits outweigh the risks of inoculation:
* Conduct counseling on the lack of evidence on the safety and efficacy of the COVID-19 vaccine in this group.
* At the end of the counseling, the health professional must deliver the Vaccine Request Form for the pregnant woman (this can be delivered digitally).
4. Available vaccines: 2 vaccines are being used in the country, one with a messenger RNA platform and the other inactivated:
* Experts believe that mRNA vaccines are safe in pregnancy and lactation as they do not contain live virus, do not produce viral replication and mRNA does not interact with the vaccinated DNA by not entering the nucleus.
* Inactivated vaccines are not contraindicated in pregnancy, for example: Influenza, dTpa. With the CoronaVac vaccine, no toxicity or teratogenicity was observed in animal models, studies that support its efficacy and safety in pregnancy are lacking.
5. ESAVI Surveillance: Monitoring of this group through a digital platform.

STRATEGY IMPLEMENTATION
✓ Pregnant women will be included in the weekly vaccination schedule.
✓ In the following weeks, pregnant women at risk for comorbidities (previously defined) will be vaccinated.
✓ Pregnant women who were inadvertently vaccinated must complete the 2-dose schedule, regardless of the time elapsed since the 1st dose.
✓ Vaccines from Pfizer Laboratories - BioNTech and Sinovac Life Sciences will be used, in a 2-dose scheme.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Pregnant women are more likely to get severely ill with COVID-19 compared to non-pregnant women.
Getting vaccinated during pregnancy can protect you from severe COVID-19 illness.
The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA),
The International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), the Royal College of Obstetricians and
Gynaecologists (RCOG), and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (ACOG) have
endorsed vaccination in pregnancy. Current data on COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy did not identify any
safety concerns for the vaccinated women or for their babies. These data in particular were from mRNA
vaccines i.e., Moderna and Pfizer BioNTech.
Similarly, several viral vector vaccines have been used in pregnancy, including large-scale Ebola vaccination trials. In these vaccination trials, there were no adverse outcomes identified in both mother and infant.
However, there is insufficient data presently on the use of viral vector vaccines for COVID-19 (J&J and
AstraZeneca). Though these vaccines are not contraindicated, administration to a pregnant or lactating
mother should be individualised and based on risk benefit assessment.
However, an mRNA vaccine is preferred if available.
Conclusion 
COVID-19 vaccines protect you from severe disease. When the risk of contracting a COVID-19 infection
outweighs the risk of the vaccine, every pregnant woman should consider getting vaccinated. 
The vaccination should be administered between 14 to 33 weeks of gestation.
Endorsed by Dr J Ravichandran R Jeganathan, Head and Senior Consultant Obstetrician
and Gynaecologist, Kementerian Kesihatan Malaysia, and Dr Murali Ganesalingam,
President, Obstetrical & Gynaecological Society of Malaysia

People who would like to have a baby
If you are trying to become pregnant now or want to get pregnant in the future, you may receive a COVID-19 vaccine when one is available to you.

....CDC does not recommend routine pregnancy testing before COVID-19 vaccination. If you are trying to become pregnant, you do not need to avoid pregnancy after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine. Like all vaccines, scientists are studying COVID-19 vaccines carefully for side effects now and will report findings as they become available.
policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Getting vaccinated is a personal choice. Any of the currently authorized COVID-19 vaccines can be offered to people who are pregnant or breastfeeding. If you have questions about getting vaccinated, a conversation with your healthcare provider might help, but is not required.

Pregnant people are at increased risk for severe illness from COVID-19
Although the overall risk of severe illness is low, pregnant people are at an increased risk for severe illness from COVID-19 when compared to non-pregnant people. Severe illness includes illness that results in intensive care admission, mechanical ventilation, or death. Additionally, pregnant people with COVID-19 might be at increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as preterm birth, compared with pregnant women without COVID-19.

Limited data are available about the safety of COVID-19 vaccines for people who are pregnant
Based on how these vaccines work in the body, experts believe they are unlikely to pose a specific risk for people who are pregnant. However, there are currently limited data on the safety of COVID-19 vaccines in pregnant people

Clinical trials that look at the safety and how well the COVID-19 vaccines work in pregnant people are underway or planned. Vaccine manufacturers are also monitoring data from people in the clinical trials who received vaccine and became pregnant.
Studies in animals receiving a Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech, or Johnson & Johnson’s Janssen (J&J/Janssen) COVID-19 vaccine before or during pregnancy found no safety concerns.
CDC and the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) have safety monitoring systems in place to gather information about vaccination during pregnancy and will closely monitor that information. Most of the pregnancies in these systems are ongoing, so we don’t yet have information on the outcomes of these pregnancies. We need to continue to follow pregnancies long-term to understand effects on pregnancy and infants.

The Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines are mRNA vaccines that do not contain the live virus that causes COVID-19 and, therefore, cannot give someone COVID-19. Additionally, mRNA vaccines do not interact with a person’s DNA or cause genetic changes because the mRNA does not enter the nucleus of the cell, which is where our DNA is kept. Learn more about how COVID-19 mRNA vaccines work.

The J&J/Janssen COVID-19 Vaccine is a viral vector vaccine, meaning it uses a modified version of a different virus (the vector) to deliver important instructions to our cells. Viral vector technology has been used by Janssen for other vaccine development programs.  Vaccines that use the same viral vector have been given to pregnant people in all trimesters of pregnancy, including in a large-scale Ebola vaccination trial. No adverse pregnancy-related outcomes, including adverse outcomes that affected the infant, were associated with vaccination in these trials. Learn more about how viral vector vaccines work.

If you are pregnant and receive a COVID-19 vaccine, consider participating in the v-safe pregnancy registry
If you are pregnant and have received a COVID-19 vaccine, we encourage you to enroll in v-safe. V-safe is CDC’s smartphone-based tool that uses text messaging and web surveys to provide personalized health check-ins after vaccination. A v-safe pregnancy registry has been established to gather information on the health of pregnant people who have received a COVID-19 vaccine. If people enrolled in v-safe report that they were pregnant at the time of vaccination or after vaccination, the registry staff might contact them to learn more. Participation is voluntary, and participants may opt out at any time.

Getting vaccinated is a personal choice
If you are pregnant, you may choose to receive a COVID-19 vaccine. You may want to have a conversation with your healthcare provider to help you decide whether to get vaccinated with a vaccine that has been authorized for use under Emergency Use Authorization. While a conversation with your healthcare provider may be helpful, it is not required prior to vaccination.

Key considerations you can discuss with your healthcare provider include:

How likely you are to being exposed to the virus that causes COVID-19
Risks of COVID-19 to you and the potential risks to your fetus or infant
What is known about the vaccine:
how well it works to develop protection in the body
known side effects of the vaccine
limited data on the safety of COVID-19 during pregnancy, because it was not studied among pregnant people
If you are pregnant and have questions about COVID-19 vaccine
If you would like to speak to someone about COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy, please contact MotherToBaby. MotherToBaby experts are available to answer questions in English or Spanish by phone or chat. The free and confidential service is available Monday–Friday 8am–5pm (local time). To reach MotherToBaby:

Call 1-866-626-6847
Chat live or send an email MotherToBabyexternal icon
Follow recommendations to prevent the spread of COVID-19 after vaccination
If you are pregnant and decide to get vaccinated, after you are fully vaccinated against COVID-19, you may be able to start doing some things that you had stopped doing because of the pandemic. Learn more about what you can do when you have been fully vaccinated.

Vaccine side effects
Side effects can occur after receiving any of the available COVID-19 vaccines, especially after the second dose for those that require two doses. Pregnant people have not reported different side effects from non-pregnant people after vaccination with mRNA vaccines (Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines). If you experience fever following vaccination you should take acetaminophen because fever has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes. Learn more at What to Expect after Getting a COVID-19 Vaccine.

Some people have experienced allergic reactions after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine. Talk with your healthcare provider if you have a history of severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to any other vaccine or injectable therapy (intramuscular, intravenous, or subcutaneous).

Key considerations you can discuss with your healthcare provider include:

The unknown risks of developing a severe allergic reaction
The benefits of vaccination
If you have an allergic reaction after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy, you can receive treatment for it.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
People who are breastfeeding
Clinical trials for the COVID-19 vaccines currently authorized for use under an Emergency Use Authorization in the United States did not include people who are breastfeeding. Because the vaccines have not been studied on lactating people, there are no data available on:

The safety of COVID-19 vaccines in lactating people
The effects of vaccination on the breastfed infant
The effects on milk production or excretion
The COVID-19 vaccines authorized now are non-replicating vaccines, meaning they are able to create an immune response but do not reproduce inside host cells. Because non-replicating vaccines pose no risk for lactating people or their infants, COVID-19 vaccines are also thought to not be a risk to the breastfeeding infant. Therefore, lactating people may choose to be vaccinated.

policies.preConceptionRecommendationFreeText:
Can women who want to have children get vaccinated against COVID-19?
Yes, women who want to have children can also be vaccinated against COVID-19. The available COVID-19 vaccines have been tested on adults - including women who want to have children - and found to be safe and effective.

Misinformation circulated, especially at the beginning of the vaccination campaign. It says vaccination can affect fertility. This statement is wrong. There is no evidence of the occurrence of infertility in the extensive clinical trials that were conducted prior to the vaccines being approved. The misinformation is based on the fact that the protein encoded by the vaccinations is structurally similar to a protein that is important for fertility. In fact, however, this similarity is limited to a few sections of the protein. Such similarities are very common and are not specific to the COVID-19 vaccination. If such a similarity made infertile, then the infection with COVID-19 would also make infertile.University of Jena ).

The Paul Ehrlich Institute assesses the security as follows: "With this data situation, the best possible security for the exclusion of damage to reproductive organs and impairment of reproduction in humans is guaranteed within the framework of a drug approval." Women who wish to have children can therefore fight against COVID -19 vaccinated (you can find more information on the subject of safety and effectiveness on the website of the Paul Ehrlich Institute ).

What women who want to have children should be aware of the vaccination during pregnancy itself. There are currently no systematic human data on whether vaccination during pregnancy is safe. That's not to say the vaccination isn't safe - there is just a lack of data to assess it. The recommendation of the Standing Vaccination Commission not to vaccinate pregnant women is based on the fact that there are not yet sufficient data for a recommendation and not that a specific risk is feared. The desire to have children is not a reason against the vaccination.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
COVID-19 vaccines and pregnancy
Talk to your obstetrician, midwife or GP about getting your COVID-19 vaccine if you are pregnant.

It's recommended you get your COVID-19 vaccine when it's offered to you. Being vaccinated will reduce the chance of you becoming very unwell.

It may also reduce the chance of complications during pregnancy. If you are seriously ill with COVID-19 during pregnancy, complications can include premature labour or stillbirths linked to COVID placentitis.

COVID-19 vaccine evidence
The COVID-19 vaccines are new and were not tested on pregnant women during clinical trials. But more than 100,000 pregnant women in the US have now had a COVID-19 vaccine. No safety concerns have been raised for these women or their babies.

The information we have so far shows that the COVID-19 vaccines do not have any negative effect on babies in the womb. Recent reports have shown that pregnant women pass on antibodies from the vaccine. This may help to protect their babies after birth.

The COVID-19 vaccines are not live vaccines, so they cannot infect either mother or baby with COVID-19. The vaccines are rapidly broken down in the body and cannot become part of your or your baby’s DNA.

Doses during pregnancy
When you get your COVID-19 vaccine, you will need 2 doses.

The 1st dose should be at or after 14 weeks of pregnancy.

The 2nd dose should be before the end of 36 weeks of pregnancy.

If the 2nd dose is not given by the end of 36 weeks, it should be delayed until after you have your baby. This is because you may get a fever after the 2nd dose.

How you will get your vaccine
Your maternity hospital will contact you to discuss your COVID-19 vaccine.

You can also talk to your obstetrician or midwife at any of your hospital appointments.

If you want to get your vaccine, they will register you and contact you about your appointment.

You will be offered a vaccination appointment within 2 to 3 weeks of being contacted.

If your next appointment is close to when you are 36 weeks pregnant, and you have not heard from your maternity hospital, contact them to discuss your options.

Where you will be vaccinated
You will be vaccinated at your maternity hospital or at a vaccination centre.

Which COVID-19 vaccine you will get
The vaccine you will be offered will depend on supply. It will be an mRNA vaccine.

The COVID-19 vaccines currently being offered to pregnant women are the:

Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine (also known as 'Comirnaty')
Moderna vaccine

If you have been vaccinated with AstraZeneca
The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for those aged 50 and older. This is because of the very rare risk of unusual blood clots with low platelets after the vaccine. These side effects are less likely to be reported after the 2nd dose of the vaccine.

If you have already had your 1st dose of the AstraZeneca vaccine, you should still get your 2nd dose. Get your 2nd dose 12 weeks after your 1st dose.

The benefits of getting your vaccine far outweigh any risks. Being fully vaccinated will reduce the chance of you becoming very unwell. These blood clots are less likely to be reported after the 2nd dose of the vaccine.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Pregnant women with COVID-19 are at higher risk of developing severe disease compared with non-pregnant women of reproductive age. While available data on vaccination of pregnant women are insufficient to assess vaccine efficacy or vaccine associated risks in pregnancy, studies are underway. Based on previous experience with other vaccine use during pregnancy, the effectiveness of the ChAdOx1-S/nCoV-19 [recombinant] vaccine in pregnant women is expected to be comparable to that observed for non-pregnant women in similar age groups. Compared with non-pregnant women, pregnancy is associated with higher rates of thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, and haemorrhage; however, it is currently not known whether pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of TTS following vaccination. In the interim, WHO recommends the use of ChAdOx1-S/nCoV-19 [recombinant] vaccine in pregnant women only if the benefits of vaccination to the pregnant woman outweigh the potential risks. To make this assessment, pregnant women should be provided with information about the risks of COVID-19 in pregnancy (including, for example, that some pregnant women are at increased risk of infection, or have comorbidities that
add to their risk of severe disease), the likely benefits of vaccination in the current epidemiological context, and the current limitations of the safety data in pregnant women. WHO does NOT recommend pregnancy testing prior to vaccination. WHO does NOT recommend delaying pregnancy or terminating pregnancy because of vaccination.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText: Breastfeeding offers substantial health benefits to lactating women and their breastfed children. Vaccine efficacy is expected to be similar in lactating women as in other adults. However, there are no data on the effects of the vaccine on breastfed children. As the ChAdOx1-S/nCoV-19 [recombinant] vaccine is not a live virus vaccine, it is biologically and clinically unlikely to pose a risk to the breastfeeding child. On the basis of these considerations, WHO recommends the use of ChAdOx1-S/nCoV-19 [recombinant] in lactating women as in other adults. WHO does NOT recommend discontinuing breastfeeding after vaccination.

Can you get a COVID-19 vaccine while pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding?

Vaccines are generally considered safe during pregnancy if they do not contain live viruses. The new mRNA and adenovirus vector COVID-19 vaccines do not contain live viruses, but, as of yet, they have not been systematically researched on people who are pregnant.  

The attending physician may, at their discretion, recommend a mRNA vaccination during pregnancy provided that the person is willing to be vaccinated and belongs to a risk group for COVID-19 due to an underlying condition or has a significant risk of being exposed to the virus at work, for example. 

COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy does not cause any particular concern or require more detailed foetal diagnostic studies. Despite the limited number of studies on pregnant women, it is presumed that the vaccination would not harm the pregnancy or the foetus. In several countries where the COVID-19 vaccination programme began earlier than in Finland, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, pregnant women have also been vaccinated on the basis of individual discretion. Data will gradually accumulate from these countries that we can also utilise in Finland.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText: You can get a COVID-19 vaccination during breastfeeding. The messenger RNA contained in the vaccine is destroyed in the body within 24 hours, and it is unlikely that it would pass into breast milk. Also the ingredients of the adenovirus vector have a short life span and are not known to transfer to human breast milk.

policies.pregnancyRecommendationFreeText:
Pregnancy and vaccination
Comirnaty and COVID-19 Vaccine Moderna
Based on increased knowledge about vaccinations against covid-19, and a special assessment of the benefit and risk of vaccination of pregnant women, a woman can be recommended vaccination starting in phase 3, even if she is pregnant. This applies in cases where the woman has any of the following conditions or diseases that may involve an increased risk of becoming seriously ill in covid-19:

Chronic cardiovascular disease, including stroke and hypertension.
Chronic lung disease such as COPD and severe and unstable asthma.
Other conditions that lead to impaired lung function or impaired cough and secretion stagnation.
Chronic liver or kidney failure.
Type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
Conditions that affect the immune system due to illness or treatment.
Pregnancy in women who are over 35 years old (born 1986 or earlier) or have a BMI over 30 (at enrollment) is always considered a risk pregnancy and they are also recommended vaccination against covid-19.

Pregnant women who before pregnancy did not have any of these risk factors, but have a pregnancy-induced disease (eg pregnancy hypertension, preeclampsia and gestational diabetes) are not included in this group which is prioritized in phase 3.

The vaccine is approved to be given throughout pregnancy, but there is usually no reason to give a vaccine during the first third of pregnancy. Thus, vaccination after the 12th week of pregnancy is recommended for this group of pregnant women. Logistics and routines when prescribing vaccination take place according to regional guidelines.

At present, the Swedish Public Health Agency is awaiting a general recommendation for vaccination for all pregnant women, but is following the development of knowledge. Vaccination can be given to fertile women without prior pregnancy testing.

According to previous decisions, mRNA vaccine ( Comirnaty or COVID-19 Vaccine Moderna ) must be offered to everyone who is 64 years and younger.
policies.lactationRecommendationFreeText:
Breastfeeding and vaccination
Comirnaty and COVID-19 Vaccine Moderna
Breast-feeding can continue even if the mother has been vaccinated against covid-19.

The product information for the various vaccines against covid-19 shows that it is unknown whether they are excreted in human milk. A negative effect of the vaccine on the breast-fed baby is not considered likely.
